summary: Specifies two extensions to the Host Identity Protocol for multi-hop routing. One allows source routing, where the sender picks nodes a packet must pass through. The other lets a packet record the nodes that forwarded it. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: One extension lets a sender write out the stops a packet must take. The other has each stop sign the packet, like a stamped passport.

subtitle: Two new HIP extensions for routing packets through multiple hops

tldr.problem: When using HIP in overlay networks, nodes need to send packets through specific intermediate nodes or record which nodes a packet passed through. Standard HIP only supported single-hop direct communication.
tldr.mechanism: Two new HIP parameters enable this: ROUTE_DST lets the sender specify nodes a packet must traverse (source routing), and ROUTE_VIA lets intermediary nodes record themselves on the packet as it passes.
tldr.outcome: Multi-hop routing in HIP is now possible, enabling applications like HIP-based overlays to control packet paths and track routing decisions.

today: RFC 6028 is an Experimental protocol and has not been obsoleted. It remains the specification for multi-hop routing extensions to HIP in overlay networks.

sections.title: Why Multi-Hop Routing in HIP
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) normally connects two hosts directly. But overlay networks—networks built on top of the internet using regular internet nodes—sometimes need packets to pass through specific intermediate nodes. This might be for finding peers, staying connected when direct paths are blocked, or controlling the flow of control traffic.

Before this extension, HIP only had a way to route through a single rendezvous server. Multi-hop routing makes it possible to specify longer paths and record where packets went.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a big network where messages sometimes need to bounce through multiple friends to reach their destination. HIP now supports that.

sections.title: Understanding the Two Extensions
sections.content:
This RFC defines two new parameters that HIP packets can carry:

ROUTE_DST (Destination List) is set by the packet's sender. It contains a list of Host Identity Tags (HITs)—the addresses of nodes the packet must visit in order. The packet goes from node to node following this list. Only the original sender can set this list, because it is protected by the sender's cryptographic signature.

ROUTE_VIA (Via List) is built as the packet travels. Each intermediate node that forwards the packet adds its own HIT to the list. This lets the destination see which nodes handled the packet. The via list is not signed by the sender, so any node on the path can add itself.
sections.plainLanguage: ROUTE_DST is like a route plan written by the sender. ROUTE_VIA is like a logbook that gets stamped at each stop.

sections.title: How Packets Follow the Lists
sections.content:
When a packet arrives at a node with a ROUTE_DST list, the node looks up its own HIT in the list. If found, the next HIT in the list becomes the next hop. If the node's HIT appears more than once, the packet is dropped to prevent forwarding loops.

Each node that forwards a packet with ROUTE_VIA should add its own HIT to the end of the list. If a node receives a packet and will send a response back, it can use the via list to create a destination list for the return path, effectively routing the response back through the same nodes in reverse order. This is called symmetric routing.

Two flags control this behavior. The SYMMETRIC flag tells the recipient that responses must use the via list as a route back. The MUST_FOLLOW flag means every node in the list must be visited in order; a node cannot skip ahead to a later node even if it has a direct path to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node checks if it is on the list. If yes, it forwards to the next node on the list. If the list says 'symmetric', replies must follow the same path back.

sections.title: The Parameter Format
sections.content:
Both ROUTE_DST and ROUTE_VIA use the same packet format. They contain a header with a 16-bit type field, a length field, a 16-bit flags field, and a variable-length list of HITs. Each HIT is 128 bits (16 bytes) long.

The format allows up to 32 HITs per parameter. ROUTE_DST must contain at least one HIT, but ROUTE_VIA can be empty when first sent (the sender starts the list, and intermediaries add to it). Since HITs are large and packets have size limits, the RFC notes that fragmentation could be an issue and recommends careful use.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it as a TLV header followed by a list of addresses. Each address is 128 bits long.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
Because ROUTE_DST is signed by the sender, an attacker cannot forge it without breaking the signature. Nodes can verify the signature to ensure the route was not tampered with.

A forged ROUTE_VIA could be used for a denial-of-service attack, but the attacker would need to know HIP nodes that form a connected path, and the maximum 32-HIT limit restricts the damage. Intermediate nodes can also limit how many HITs they accept or which HITs are allowed.

A malicious node could create a destination list with the same HIT appearing twice, causing a forwarding loop. But nodes check for this and drop such packets. Additional protection using a time-to-live-like mechanism is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender signs the destination list so nobody can change it. If someone tries to create a loop, the packet gets dropped.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in octets, number-of-HITs times 16 plus 4
